title: Elon Musk, the world’s richest man, says he’s living in an Airstream trailer to oversee xAI’s biggest expansion yet
description: Musk says he is living at xAI’s Memphis data center site, continuing a longtime habit of sleeping where he works.
fullText:
Elon Musk, the world's richest man, has some new digs—an Airstream trailer in Memphis, parked just steps from xAI's most ambitious project yet.

Musk, who has a net worth of $917 billion according to the Bloomberg Billionaire Index and became the world's first trillionaire for 12 days in June, said Monday he was in his new "palace" as he spoke during a taping of the All-In podcast alongside Gwynne Shotwell, the president and chief operating officer of SpaceX.

Shotwell, for her part, praised Musk's latest unusual home as an example of his long history of committing fully to projects he cares about throughout his career.

"This is Elon, by the way, doing what people don't believe he does. He sleeps on the factory floor. He's in Memphis, helping build buildings," she said during the interview.

Musk is in Memphis as xAI races to expand Colossus, a massive supercomputer center that has provided it with so much computing power that it has struck deals to provide excess capacity to Google and Anthropic for billions. The company started building Colossus in 2024 to provide compute for Grok, xAI's large language model, and the initial build reportedly took only 122 days.

While putting a data center in space could still be far off, Memphis has emerged as the center of xAI's infrastructure buildout here on Earth. In late July, the company announced it would build a fourth data center called Minihard that will add to its other facilities.

Musk did not say which Airstream model he was living in, but some of the aluminum-shelled campers pack a sleeping area, kitchen, and bathroom into a 16-foot space.

Still, Musk has been known to want to sleep close to the action when a new project interested him or required his direct attention. When Musk and his brother Kimbal were building their first startup, Zip2, in the '90s, they slept in a tiny Palo Alto office for six months while showering at the YMCA, according to Walter Isaacson's biography of Musk.

Even as a newfound multi-millionaire, having received $22 million from selling Zip2 to Compaq, Musk slept under his desk most nights as he prepared to launch X.com, the online bank that would later become PayPal, in 1999, according to Isaacson's biography.

Even when he rose to the rank of super wealthy, having received another approximately $175 million from eBay's acquisition of PayPal, he often stayed at colleagues' homes while traveling in Silicon Valley, including the home of Michael Marks, who briefly served as Tesla CEO in 2007 before the pair clashed and Musk later took over the role.

title: Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte appears in court in The Hague
description: Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte, who is facing charges of crimes against humanity at the International Criminal Court, made his first public appearance in more than a year on Wednesday, wh...
fullText:
THE HAGUE, Netherlands (AP) — Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte, who is facing charges of crimes against humanity at the International Criminal Court, made his first public appearance in more than a year on Wednesday, when he attended a pretrial hearing at the court in The Hague.

The 81-year old is accused of murder and attempted murder for his alleged involvement in dozens of killings as part of his so-called war on drugs while in office, first as the mayor of a southern city in the Philippines and later as president. He denies the charges against him.

He has missed a series of hearings since his arrest in 2025. Medical reasons were cited for his absence but the court's judges ruled in January that he was healthy enough to stand trial.

The presiding judge in his case told Duterte's legal team during an earlier hearing that she wanted the ex-leader to attend Wednesday's session.

"We would expect Mr. Duterte to be here unless there's some medical issue," Judge Joanna Korner said during the June pretrial hearing.

Wednesday's hearing is to discuss evidence disclosure and come up with a timetable for the trial, which is due to open in November.

Duterte was arrested in March 2025 and was set to appear in court in The Hague in September last year. However, the hearing was delayed after a pretrial panel of judges granted a "limited postponement" to give the court time to determine whether Duterte was fit enough to take part in the proceedings.

Following an assessment by a panel of medical experts, judges ruled that Duterte is "fit to take part in the pretrial proceedings."

The ICC has been looking into mass killings in crackdowns overseen by Duterte since 2018. Estimates of the death toll during Duterte's presidential term vary, from the more than 6,000 that the national police have reported up to 30,000 claimed by human rights groups.

According to the prosecutors, police and government hit squads carried out dozens of killings at Duterte's orders, motivated by the promise of money or to avoid becoming targets themselves.

A month after the court in February 2018 announced a preliminary investigation into the violent drug crackdowns, Duterte said the Philippines would withdraw from the ICC.

Last year, judges rejected a request from Duterte's legal team to throw out the case because of the Philippine withdrawal. Countries cannot "abuse" their right to withdraw from the court's foundational Rome Statute "by shielding persons from justice in relation to alleged crimes that are already under consideration," the decision says.

Earlier this year, an attempt by authorities to arrest another man wanted by the ICC in connection with the drug killings dissolved into gunfire in the Philippine Senate in May. No one was hurt. The court had unsealed an arrest warrant for Ronald Marapon dela Rosa, who served as national police chief under Duterte. Dela Rosa went into hiding following the Senate standoff and remains on the run.

Two months later, the Philippine Senate, acting as an impeachment court, opened the trial of Duterte's daughter, Vice President Sara Duterte. If convicted of the charges, which include amassing unexplained wealth and publicly threatening the family of the current president, Ferdinand Marcos Jr., she may be permanently disqualified from holding public office. She denies the charges.

title: Messi in Argentina squad for farewell friendly
description: Argentina name Lionel Messi in their squad for a friendly against Benin in October in a match which is set to be the forward's farewell to international football.
fullText:
Argentina have named Lionel Messi in their squad for a friendly against Benin in October in a match which is set to be the forward's farewell to international football.

Messi announced his retirement from Argentina duty in August in the wake of his country's defeat by Spain in the 2026 World Cup final and after saying he was considering his future in football following the death of his father, Jorge.

The 39-year-old, who captained Argentina when they won the 2022 World Cup, said the decision to stop playing for La Albiceleste hurt him "deeply" but that he had "given it my all" and had "nothing left to give".

Messi, an eight-time Ballon d'Or winner who currently plays for Inter Miami, is Argentina's all-time leading scorer and most-capped player, having scored 125 goals in 207 appearances.

"We made the decision to invite the best player in the world, the symbol of our national team, our captain, Lionel Andres Messi, so that he can have the farewell he truly deserves on 6 October here in Argentina," said Argentine FA president Claudio Tapia.

River Plate's Estadio Monumental in Buenos Aires, which has an 85,000 capacity, will host the game against Benin.

Argentina's 2022 World Cup winners have also been invited to the match, which Tapia said would be an "unforgettable" occasion.

Argentina were ordered to play their next two home matches with 50% capacity, although one match of that sanction was suspended, for breaches of the Fifa disciplinary code during the World Cup.

The punishment related to using a sports event for demonstrations of a non-sporting nature, team misconduct, and discriminatory chants and gestures by its supporters.

After defeating England 2-1 in the World Cup semi-final, several Argentina players held up a banner claiming Argentine sovereignty over the Falkland Islands, a British overseas territory.

As they play friendlies against Bolivia on 30 September in Cordoba and Burkina Faso in Buenos Aires on 3 October, it should mean the punishment will have been served before the Benin game.

Argentina midfielder Leandro Paredes and team-mate Nahuel Molina are not expected to be available as they were given respective 10-game and seven-match suspensions for their part in on-field clashes following their country's defeat by Spain in the World Cup final.

title: How Kenya won its bid for 2029 World Athletics Championships
description: Kenya's athletics-loving population and improved infrastructure helped Nairobi secure the rights to host the 2029 World Championships, but challenges remain to ensure a successful event.
fullText:
Kenya's President William Ruto says the World Athletics Championship will be "coming home", with Nairobi set to make history after being selected as the first African city to host the event in 2029.

Ruto hailed the winning bid as a "victory for generations of athletes" who have made the nation "synonymous with excellence" on the track and road.

Nairobi beat London and Rome to the hosting rights, with Munich selected to stage the 2031 edition.

After missing out on the 2025 World Championships to Tokyo, a series of factors helped Kenya see off its European rivals this time around.

When World Athletics president Lord Coe announced the decision in Budapest on Tuesday, he described Kenya's bid as "compelling and emotional".

The East African nation is the second-most successful nation in the history of the World Championships with 72 gold medals, placing it behind the United States.

The vast majority of those glories, alongside 38 Olympic gold medals, have come in middle- and long-distance running.

Lord Coe said that athletics is "woven into the fabric" of the nation and that Kenyans have helped "shape the history" of the sport.

He name-checked several runners including two-time Olympic champion Eliud Kipchoge - who was involved in the lobbying for Kenya's bid - men's 800m world record holder David Rudisha and multiple world and Olympic medallist Faith Kipyegon.

A passionate fanbase is also one of the country's great strengths.

Some 68% of Kenyans surveyed by World Athletics rated their interest in athletics as high, compared with a global average of 39%.

Athletics is the country's second-most followed sport, behind only football, and when World Athletics assessed its social media channels, Kenya was the fourth-highest nation in terms of followers.

Kenya's previous bid for the 2025 edition fell down largely on the facilities which the country possessed.

This time around, the Kasarani Stadium will have gone through a complete structural upgrade well before the world's top athletes descend on Nairobi.

The 48,000-capacity venue will be used when Kenya co-hosts football's 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) next June and July alongside Tanzania and Uganda.

"We learned from the 2025 bid because there were areas that we did not score well," Barnaba Korir, who worked on the successful bid, told the BBC World Service.

"Because of that, we managed to improve on those areas.

"I'm happy that the infrastructure that we have already developed will also meet the standards that we have seen all over the world."

Hotel space is one area not expected to be a problem, with Nairobi a regular host for large conventions.

"Kenya is also known for its very dynamic hospitality, the tourism sector," Elijah Mwangi, principal secretary at the State Department for Sports, told the BBC.

"It has a game park within the city, so we are waiting to welcome everybody."

President Ruto made financial and security guarantees in order to secure the Championships.

"We thank World Athletics for the confidence it has placed in Kenya," Ruto said.

"We will honour that confidence by delivering an unforgettable championship worthy of our athletes, our country and our continent."

Lord Coe became president of World Athletics (then known as the IAAF) in 2015 and has pledged to grow the sport around the globe.

During his time in office the World Championships have been hosted in Qatar (2019), the United States (2022) and Tokyo, while China's capital Beijing will stage them in 2027.

Kenya has successfully hosted age-grade events in Nairobi and the World Cross Country Championships in Mombasa, while the World Athletics Relays were held in Botswana's capital Gaborone in May.

With Coe's third term in office coming to an end next year, one official involved in Kenya's bid, speaking before the host announcement, said it was "unthinkable" that Nairobi would not succeed.

"With this decision we continue to fulfil our mission of growing athletics worldwide," Coe said.

"It was important that the World Athletics Championships should come to Africa when we had the right host, the right bid and the right circumstances.

Coe hailed the "quality, ambition and commitment" of all four bidding cities.

London, Munich and Rome have all previously held the Olympics, with the World Championships in London as recently as 2017, but the chance to break new ground in Africa was clearly compelling.

UK Athletics chief executive Jack Buckner said his team was "deeply disappointed" to see London miss out.

Kenya now faces logistical and organisational challenges over the next three years as it prepares to deliver Africa's first World Championships.

With the 2027 Afcon looming large on the horizon, Nairobi will have a chance to test-run getting fans in and out of the Kasarani Stadium, which lies about a half-hour drive from the city's central business district.

The venue does not have any rail connections but Korir says World Athletics officials were "very satisfied" by Kenya's transport plan.

There were instances of overcrowding when the stadium hosted Kenya games at football's African Nations Championships last year, which led to the capacity being reduced for some matches.

Delays in preparations for Afcon have raised concerns, and the funding for the World Championships will come entirely from the Kenyan government.

Mwangi revealed that $78m (£58.5m) is the current estimate for the government's contribution, with sponsorship deals also playing a role.

"We are prepared to ensure that whatever is expected to be paid, it is paid in the due time," he added.

Presidential elections are scheduled for next year, but Korir is confident organisers will secure the "huge" and "legally binding" figure earmarked even if there is a change in government.

"Whatever the government assigns now will be observed by the next government. It is an international agreement," he said.

Then comes ticketing, first to make sure the local population are not priced out and then to ensure the stands are filled.

The cheapest tickets for the Under-18 World Championships in 2017 were priced at 200 Kenyan shillings ($1.15, £1.14) but attendances were low until entry was made free.

World Athletics generated $522m in revenue from Tokyo 2025, with a total of 619,000 tickets sold over the nine days of competition, while London sold a record 705,000 tickets in 2017.

In passing up the opportunity of returning to the British capital, World Athletics has chosen expansion over guaranteed ticket sales, but attendances will be scrutinised - especially after the sparse numbers seen in the stands in Doha in 2019.

Korir, however, is confident the Kasarani Stadium "will be full" on "every day" of competition, including morning sessions, if sales begin early enough.

Meanwhile, Kenya has endured a spate of doping scandals in recent years, with 11 individuals banned by the Athletics Integrity Unit so far this year alone.

The pressure is now on the East African nation to deliver on its promises in the build-up to Nairobi 2029 and ensure the Championships pass off without any major issues.

title: Tuchel regrets not eating Azteca turf after win over Mexico
description: Thomas Tuchel regrets not eating any of the grass at the Azteca Stadium after England's epic World Cup win against Mexico.
fullText:
Thomas Tuchel regrets not eating any of the grass at the Azteca Stadium after England's World Cup win against Mexico.

His Three Lions beat the co-hosts 3-2 in the last-16 tie in July, despite playing much of the second half with 10 men following Jarell Quansah's red card.

England went on to reach the semi-finals, where they lost to Argentina, before beating France in the Bronze medal match for third place.

Tuchel, though, made a bizarre admission during an interview with Daniel Sturridge for the FA's forthcoming feature 'Reflections: England's World Cup Journey'.

He said: "I texted a friend after the match and I just wrote, 'I regret that I didn't eat some grass after the match to keep something from this in my body forever'. That was the feeling. That was the moment.

England's victory was only the third time Mexico had tasted defeat at the stadium in 90 competitive matches.

Tuchel described it as one of the highlights of the campaign and hailed the "huge bond" within the camp, especially the reaction to Jordan Henderson's tournament-ending injury after falling over an advertising hoarding while celebrating the Azteca success.

"This game had so much of what you could wish for," added the German. "If you needed any proof of what it meant to these players and how they were with each other, it was the moment Jordan fell over and broke his arm.

"Within a second, the players were there. Every single player was there stopping the celebrations, building a shield, protecting Jordan, not going anywhere, in full empathy. It was so special."

England are next in action against World Cup winners Spain on 26 September in their 2026-27 Uefa Nations League opener, with the 2028 European Championships also on Tuchel's radar.

Confident of ending England's wait for a first senior men's trophy since 1966, he believed their World Cup run not only cemented his relationship with the squad - "it feels like they are my players now" - but also represented "something to build on".

Tuchel added: "I'm very excited. I think we got another step closer and I think we're there."

title: Iran's regime came for teenage twins. Their fate offers a glimpse of Tehran's widening death campaign
description: Iranian twins Taraneh and Romina Rahimi face execution and decades in prison after joining protests, as Iran's death penalty surge draws global alarm.
fullText:
Taraneh and Romina Rahimi were 19, still in high school and living with their mother when masked men came for them in the middle of the night.

According to their U.S.-based cousin, the twin sisters were dragged from their beds with bags placed over their heads about a month after they joined anti-regime protests in Isfahan. Their family was given no explanation and spent months searching courts, hospitals and government offices trying to determine where they had been taken.

Four months later, their mother, Marzieh Nourmohammadi, was finally allowed to see them at Dowlatabad Prison. She barely recognized her daughters.

One Glaring Issue Goes Unaddressed In Un Chief's High-stakes Talks With Iran's President

Their cousin, Masoud Nourmohammadi, told The Guardian that the twins had badly swollen and bruised faces, injuries to their elbows, hands and feet, and significant hair loss that he said resulted from guards pulling them by their hair as they were moved between cells. He said their mother also learned that the sisters had been held in solitary confinement.

Now 20, Taraneh Rahimi faces execution over her alleged role in the January protests, while her twin sister could spend decades in prison, in a case unfolding amid a sharp rise in Iran's use of the death penalty.

Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA) reported that Taraneh was sentenced to death and an additional 11 years in prison, while Romina received a 36-year sentence. The sentences were issued by Branch 1 of the Isfahan Revolutionary Court and remain initial-stage verdicts.

The twins are among 16 defendants prosecuted in what has become known as the "Isfahan Shohada Square" case. HRANA said 10 defendants received death sentences and the 16 defendants collectively received 256 years in prison.

The sisters' family says the abuse was intended to force confessions.

Iran Jails Psychologist Over Trump Plea As Regime Demands He Make Americans 'Look Stupid': Family

Nourmohammadi told The Guardian that Taraneh was threatened that prison guards would rape Romina in front of her unless she signed a confession. The outlet reported that Taraneh later told the court that admissions attributed to her had been obtained through torture. Her mother was not permitted to attend the trial, according to the family.

Radio Farda separately reported, citing Nourmohammadi, that the sisters suffered physical and psychological abuse and were forced to confess to accusations they deny. The Hana Human Rights Organization told Fox News Digital they have verified the torture allegations.

Concerns about torture extend beyond the sisters. HRANA reported that another defendant in the same case, Ahmadreza Saeidi, told judges during the hearing that the investigating judge personally used an electric stun gun on his neck and genitals. Defense lawyers also reportedly complained that they had not been given access to substantial portions of the case file or adequate time to examine evidence before trial.

The sentences come as rights organizations document a sharp rise in executions across Iran.

Could Narges Mohammadi Unite Iran's Opposition? Husband Says Imprisoned Nobel Laureate Still Fighting

The Washington-based Abdorrahman Boroumand Center for Human Rights in Iran documented 901 executions during the first seven months of 2026, including 56 people executed on political or national-security charges.

Behnam Ben Taleblu, Iran program senior director at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told Fox News Digital that the executions should be viewed as part of a broader campaign by Tehran to suppress dissent at home.

"Despite the war in the region, despite the drone war, the missile war, the war over the Strait of Hormuz, the real war is the one that's happening on a day-to-day basis inside the Islamic Republic," Ben Taleblu said. "The Islamic Republic is quite literally cracking skulls, cracking down on civil society, on dissidents, on protesters."

Among those imprisoned in Iran's broader crackdown is Seyed Ahmad Seyedabdollahi, a 32-year-old psychologist whose case Fox News Digital reported in August.

Seyedabdollahi posted an English-language video on Jan. 4 appealing directly to President Donald Trump to support Iranian protesters, according to his relatives and Fox News Digital's previous reporting. He was arrested 10 days later and ultimately sentenced to seven months in prison and barred from government and public services for five years.

His relatives told Fox News Digital that Iranian authorities later pressured him to record another video insulting Trump and Americans and alleged that he was subjected to solitary confinement and torture.

The Hana Human Rights Organization reported Aug. 9 that Seyedabdollahi had been held in Borujen Prison since July 7 and that authorities opened a second case against him on a charge of "propaganda against the system of the Islamic Republic." Hana also confirmed that he was serving a seven-month sentence and had received a five-year disqualification from public and governmental services.

His relatives confirmed to Fox News Digital that authorities have continued pressuring him to say he was a "foreign agent" paid by the U.S. government. They also said authorities revoked his professional license, adding financial pressure on his family.

Ben Taleblu said Tehran has followed a similar pattern after previous periods of external conflict, turning its attention inward against perceived opponents.

Inside Tehran: Iranians Describe Irgc's Brutal Rule, Poverty — Ask Trump To 'Stay The Course'

"We saw this trend in the aftermath of the 12-day war as well," Ben Taleblu said. "Lose a war abroad, come home and pretend like you're the victor."

"Simply here, the Islamic Republic is continuing the longest war it's ever fought, which is the 47-year war against the Iranian people," he added.

Wednesday marks four years since the Sept. 16, 2022, death of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish Iranian woman who was detained three days earlier by Iran's morality police over what authorities described as "improper hijab." Her death sparked nationwide protests that became known internationally as the "Woman, Life, Freedom" movement. The U.N. said reports that Amini had been beaten in custody warranted an independent investigation, while Iranian authorities maintained that she died of "natural causes."

'Killing Off The Country': Iran Executes Dozens, Arrests 4,000-Plus In War Crackdown

The 2022 uprising was itself part of a longer cycle of unrest. Nationwide demonstrations beginning in December 2017 rapidly spread across Iran and represented the largest challenge to the government since the 2009 Green Movement. The 2017-18 protests were followed by another major nationwide wave in 2019 and then the 2022 Woman, Life, Freedom uprising.

Ben Taleblu argued that whenever another major protest movement emerges, Western governments should be prepared to help Iranians communicate with one another and the outside world, particularly when authorities shut down internet access.

"We know every single time another major protest is happening, the way the regime cracks down is to first turn off the internet," he said. "That means the regime fears what comes of coordination between Iranians and fears what comes of when the Iranians are able to send their message outside to the international community."

"The partners of the Iranian people, America, Israel, the West, these are largely all cyber superpowers," Ben Taleblu said. "We should not let the Iranian people continue to die in the darkness."

title: As the world debates the risks of AI, China closes the technology gap with the US
description: As the rapid development of artificial intelligence triggers a renewed debate about its risks, the United States and China keep racing to develop increasingly powerful models even as they express thei...
fullText:
HONG KONG (AP) — As the rapid development of artificial intelligence triggers a renewed debate about its risks, the United States and China keep racing to develop increasingly powerful models even as they express their own concerns.

The U.S. has outpaced China and other countries for years in AI model capabilities, research, citations and other areas. But China has been rapidly catching up as an AI superpower even as U.S.-led restrictions have blocked China from accessing some of the most advanced technologies, including the cutting-edge chips and the machines to make them.

Experts and recent reports, like one by the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence, said China has emerged as an AI counterweight to the U.S. and this year appears to be erasing the U.S. lead.

"The gap between U.S. and Chinese models is narrow and fragile," said Samm Sacks, a senior fellow at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies' Institute for America, China, and the Future of Global Affairs.

The current debate takes on greater importance ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping's expected visit to Washington this month to meet U.S. President Donald Trump, and as experts say the future of AI will depend significantly on what China and the U.S. do and don't do.

Here's a quick look at some of the most important Chinese AI models and the concerns in both Washington and Beijing:

Beijing-based startup Moonshot AI made a splash with the release of Kimi K3, taking Silicon Valley by surprise with capabilities close to U.S. rivals. It was ranked No. 3 globally in model intelligence in July, shortly after its release, behind Anthropic's Claude Fable 5 and OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol, according to AI benchmarking platform Artificial Analysis. But Kimi K3 now ranks ninth, behind new frontier models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta and SpaceXAI, indicating China's AI lead is fluid.

AI startup darling DeepSeek was the first to upend global stock markets by proving Chinese AI models are capable of challenging the U.S. lead. The company's R1 model, released in January 2025, was more cost-effective than similar U.S. models. In April, DeepSeek previewed its powerful V4 model, saying it has big improvements in knowledge, reasoning and "agentic" capabilities, referring to the ability to plan and execute multiple, complex steps with limited human guidance.

The powerful GLM-5.2 from startup Z.ai that rolled out in June raised Silicon Valley eyebrows with comparisons to the most advanced Anthropic and OpenAI models. Z.ai then launched GLM-5.3 in August with improved coding and agentic capabilities that pushed it up the global AI model rankings.

In July, China's Alibaba previewed its Qwen3.8-Max model, which the tech giant said was its most powerful model in the series, challenging Anthropic's Claude Fable and OpenAI's GPT.

China's state security minister has warned artificial intelligence poses a range of potential threats to the country, from political and ideological security to cyberattacks, data leaks and challenges to governance.

In an article published Sunday, Chen Yixin said the technology could threaten China's political, institutional, and ideological security if used by "hostile forces and individuals with ulterior motives."

Some individuals might use AI-generated deepfake audio and video to create "political rumors" on a massive scale, he wrote.

Chen specifically mentioned the capabilities of Anthropic's Claude and OpenAI's GPT as examples of how AI could be used to more easily identify and "weaponize" cybersecurity vulnerabilities. He warned certain nations and groups can now "execute complex hacking tasks."

Top Chinese leaders have said China should accelerate the AI development and pursue technological self-reliance. But they also noted the need to control the risks and establish a global framework for AI governance.

The U.S. has accused China's AI developers of engaging in what it has called "industrial-scale distillation," in which AI models are trained to copy or imitate the capabilities of more powerful ones.

In the most comprehensive report by the government to date, the FBI and the National Security Agency and Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency said Sept. 8 that Chinese AI developers extracted capabilities from some of the most advanced AI models in the U.S. in "aggressive, malicious, and targeted distillation activities."

Also on Sept. 8, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told an event that "the Chinese distill our models and they can never get ahead of us."

China has rejected the claims and said distillation is commonly used across many AI companies. It asked the United States to refrain from making "unfounded accusations" and accused the U.S. of pursuing a "monopoly of the AI industry."

Distillation is a standard technique used across the AI industry, but the U.S. agencies leveled a more specific accusation that Chinese firms used unauthorized access and other methods to extract restricted capabilities from American frontier models, said Lizzi C. Lee, a fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute's Center for China Analysis.

"These are still contested allegations at this point but I think the strategic implication is already important," she said.

The United States spent a lot energy into controlling the inputs into frontier AI, especially chips. But now "it seems that it is finally discovering that it may also have to think about the outputs of frontier AI as a form of technology transfer," Lee said.

"The U.S. labs spend enormous amounts of compute pushing out the frontier. But Chinese developers can learn from those systems," she said. "And Chinese companies then (can) release very capable open-weight models that spread globally."

Castillo reported from Beijing.

title: McDermott wants to commit to England for 2030 World Cup
description: Brian McDermott says he wants to stay on as England's head coach for the 2030 Rugby League World Cup.
fullText:
Brian McDermott says he wants to stay on as England's head coach for the 2030 Rugby League World Cup.

The former Leeds Rhinos head coach, 56, was appointed on a short-term agreement in April to guide England through this autumn's World Cup, which is taking place in Australia, New Zealand and Papua New Guinea.

McDermott said when he started in the job that he would be interested in staying on beyond the tournament.

And although he has made clear that he wants to focus on the immediate task of seeking success this October and November, he does want to commit to his country for the long term if all goes well.

He said: "Well, we've had a very informal discussion about what that might look like and then that's all it is. And it's been a really short conversation.

"Clearly, I'd like to do the job for longer. I'd like to get another crack at the World Cup in four years' time.

"You know, if you're going to do this properly, give me four years' preparation, where we're building it up year by year and getting players connected to a programme which has got a start, a middle and the end."

McDermott, currently working as an assistant coach at NRL club Gold Coast Titans, has taken the England role on a part-time basis, in contrast to his full-time predecessor Shaun Wane.

He has confirmed Wigan great Sean O'Loughlin and St Helens legend Paul Wellens as assistant coaches for the World Cup.

And he believes England are well set for it, but having had only a limited time to prepare - with no matches before their World Cup opener against Tonga in Perth on 17 October - he would like a chance to have a full build-up to a major tournament.

He said: "This has been a crazy, crazy period over the last few months to try and coordinate all this. And I think we're in good shape, by the way.

"But yeah, I've made it no secret. I'd like a crack at the next World Cup and a four-year build-up to that.

"We haven't gone too deep into those discussions. And when you mention it, you think, no, let's not talk about that. I've got to get my mind on this here. So it has been mentioned, but I'm not chasing that just yet."

Rhinos dominate 2026 Super League Dream Team

McDermott said when he took the job that he intended to stick with George Williams as captain.

The Warrington half-back, who will leave Super League for NRL club Dolphins after the World Cup, returned to action in August after four months out with a neck injury.

Having got to know Williams during that time, McDermott is happy to have him leading the team.

"He's been great to speak to," McDermott said. "I didn't really know George at all.

"It's been really enjoyable to get to know him. He's keen as anything.

"And while he was injured, you could just tell he came back from injury early, but you could tell if there's anybody who's going to come back from it early, it would be him.

"And I'm really pleased to see the form that he's in now.

"His leadership's been really good. When we've had the groups meetings, I saw the way he would speak on there and just have a bit of maturity.

title: Eligibility rules 'not particularly fair' - O'Neill
description: Northern Ireland manager Michael O'Neill says what upsets him the most regarding rules over international eligibility is the pressure put on young players to make an irreversible choice.
fullText:
Northern Ireland manager Michael O'Neill said what upsets him the most regarding rules over international eligibility is the pressure put on young players to make an irreversible choice.

Any player born in Northern Ireland is also eligible to play for the Republic of Ireland, but Fifa rules state that an application to transfer international allegiance can only be made once.

The situation has again been in the spotlight with regards to Arsenal teenager Ceadach O'Neill who has won two senior caps for Northern Ireland and on Tuesday was included in the squad for a Nations League quadruple-header, but has also been subject to an approach from the Republic of Ireland.

At present, the player would be required to undertake a Fifa transfer of international allegiance should he wish to play for the Republic of Ireland at any level, but if he makes an appearance in the upcoming Nations League quadruple header, would have to wait until he is 21 to do so. Should he reach four caps, he would be unable to transfer at any stage.

"My focus is on the player, and I have a duty of care to the player as his international manager, as we have as an association as well," said Michael O'Neill.

"He's been in our pathway since he's been a young boy. He's been part of our academy. He's obviously had an approach from another association, which happens.

"The thing that upsets me the most in this is that putting a young player in a position to make an international transfer before he's been a professional for even two years is, I think, not the right thing. It's not something that any association should be doing."

O'Neill and Graham retain places in NI squad

Arsenal have 'big hopes' for O'Neill - Arteta

Under the Good Friday Agreement - the 1998 peace accord that followed the conflict colloquially known as The Troubles - those born in Northern Ireland can hold both British and Irish passports.

A Court of Arbitration for Sport ruling in 2010 means players born anywhere on the island of Ireland are able to represent the Republic of Ireland regardless of whether they fulfil any other measure of eligibility, namely being born in the territory, having a biological mother, father, grandmother or grandfather born in the territory, or having lived there for an uninterrupted period of five years.

Players born in the Republic of Ireland, however, cannot represent Northern Ireland unless they are otherwise eligible.

"We exploit eligibility, the same as every other country does, down to the grandparent rule, but this is a rule which is obviously unique between ourselves and the FAI [Football Association of Ireland]," said O'Neill.

"I think everyone recognises it's not particularly fair, but as I say, our focus is to make sure our pathway for our young players is as good as possible and that's a pathway for boys from any part of the community."

In May, FAI director of football John Martin said the organisation should at "the bare minimum" be sounding out eligible players.

"We know there are kids out there who want to play for Ireland who haven't been approached in the past," said Martin.

"That's not right. It's making sure we have a presence and we understand all the players available to us, and that they are being monitored and tracked."

When asked whether the narrative around young players in or around his squad is tiresome to him, O'Neill said: "It would have been in the past, it's not tiresome now.

"We have people who comment on this and talk about nationality and talk about identity and talk about all these different things, which are part of being born in Northern Ireland and growing up in Northern Ireland.

"But I think what we're missing now is that we're putting young players in a situation where they have to make a decision which is irreversible."

During O'Neill's time as manager, Tottenham Hotspur's Jamie Donley and Gillingham's Ronan Hale have made international transfers to Northern Ireland from England and the Republic of Ireland respectively.

"We've done two international transfers in my time. Jamie Donley, who is now a senior international, and Ronan Hale, who was 25 at the time when we asked him to make that decision," added O'Neill.

"I think there's a point in a player's career where you've just got to let him play and develop, enjoy his football without creating a situation like this.

"We haven't created this situation. Ceadach's been in our system all along and he's in our squad now."

While James McClean and Shane Duffy are the two most prominent examples of players who made the switch from Northern Ireland at underage level and went on to have long international careers for the Republic of Ireland, O'Neill believes others would have won considerably more caps for his side.

"I think if you look at it from our point of view, there's not many players that have been a success who have gone from Northern Ireland," he said.

"I can think of two, James McClean and Shane Duffy, who had international careers where they got over 50 caps. Otherwise, most of the other players who have gone that route have not played consistently or not had, I think, possibly the international career they could have had if they stayed here.

"It is a decision for the player to make, ultimately, and we have to respect that, but as I've said all along, I think there's two sides to this. There is obviously who you feel you should play for, but there's also the situation around a football decision where you can have longevity in your international career."

title: Pidcock and Backstedt lead GB at Road Worlds

Tom Pidcock and Zoe Backstedt will lead Great Britain's challenge at the 2026 Road World Championships.

The races for the coveted rainbow jerseys take place in Montreal, Canada, from 20-27 September, live across the BBC.

The championships include both the road race and time trial disciplines, with Pinarello Q36.5's Pidcock leading the men's team in the road race, while Ethan Hayter races in the men's time trial.

Backstedt steps up to the elite category after winning last year's Under-23 race and is joined by Anna Morris, 31, who has won a number of domestic races in 2026.

Performance director for British Cycling Stephen Park said: "The Road World Championships are always one of the standout events in the cycling calendar, and we are excited to return with a highly competitive squad.

title: Draper decides not to play again this season
description: Former world number four Jack Draper will not play again this season, but says he is aiming to return to the tour at the start of next year.
fullText:
Former world number four Jack Draper will not play again this season, but says he is aiming to return to the tour at the start of next year.

The 24-year-old has been suffering with bone bruising in his serving arm and has only played nine events since last year's Wimbledon.

Draper missed the US Open, after losing in the first round in Montreal and Cincinnati last month - and was in tears during his defeat to France's Terence Atmane in Canada.

"I am taking this time to reset and heal so when I return I am 100% ready to go," Draper posted on Instagram., external

"Tennis is my purpose and passion and so when I step back on court I want to make sure that there's nothing holding me back from where I want to go."

Why can't Draper play, and why won't surgery help?

Tearful Draper struggles during comeback defeat

Draper will not qualify for a protected ranking if he does return in January, as only those who are out for over six months are able to retain the ranking they had when they left the tour.

He is currently ranked 155, which means he would require wildcards or have to come through qualifying to play in Grand Slams and ATP Tour events.

But none of that will worry him if he is able to play freely and without so much pain.

Draper peaked at four in the world last June after winning a first Masters 1000 title in Indian Wells and finishing runner-up at another in Madrid.

"Last summer, all the dedication and work I had put into this sport was coming together," Draper added.

"It was all going my way and the path seemed so clear. However a complicated injury made things incredibly challenging, and since that moment I've been desperately trying to get back and feel as I once did on the court.

"Managing so much change, adversity and pain has helped me to grow massively in many areas of my life but has also made me feel a level of fatigue."

Draper has taken a holiday with friends in recent weeks and has been trying to aid his recovery by taking a mental break from the sport.

He is expected to make a gradual return to training over the next few weeks, as his team try to work out the principal causes of the injury.

Draper used to play with polyester strings, but has been experimenting with natural gut - which is against his instincts, but should ease the burden on his arm.

He has also started using a lighter racquet, and is making some changes to his serve. Diet is another area being examined to see if that, too, could be a contributing factor.

Andy Murray remains part of his coaching team but will do a limited number of weeks on the road, and so further assistance will be required.

Over the summer, Draper benefitted from the help of LTA coaches James Trotman (who was with him full-time as he rose into the world's top five) and Alex Lisiecki.

A permanent coach to work alongside Murray will need to be found, however, once Draper returns to the tour.

When he does, much thought will go into his schedule. Not just because the bone bruising is unlikely to have healed entirely by January, but also because of the concerns many top players have about the toll the modern game is putting on their bodies.

London loses out to Nairobi in bid to host 2029 World Athletics Championships
description: Nairobi, Kenya will be the first African host of athletics’ biggest event outside the Olympic Games
fullText:
London has lost out on hosting rights for the 2029 World Athletics Championships, with the event instead to be held in Africa for the first time.

Nairobi, Kenya submitted the winning bid, beating other candidate cities Rome, London and Munich for the rights to host athletics' biggest event outside the Olympic Games.

The hosts for the next two editions were announced in a World Athletics conference in Budapest, which has just hosted the inaugural Ultimate Championships, on Tuesday.

World Athletics president Seb Coe said "the interest in hosting our world championships has frankly never been higher" and praised "the quality, commitment and ambition demonstrated by all four... outstanding bids".

He said: "Taking our championships to Africa for the first time will be historic. Nairobi has presented a compelling and an emotional bid.

"This is a fast-growing, dynamic, modern metropolis that serves as the economic, cultural, and political hub of East Africa.

"Kenya is one of the great athletics nations. The sport is woven into the fabric of the country, and athletes such as world gold medallists Faith Kipyegon, Vivian Cheruiyot, Eliud Kipchoge, Hellen Obiri and David Rudisha, as well as two-time Olympic champion Kip Keino, multiple world cross-country champion Paul Tergat and multiple world half marathon champion Tegla Loroupe, have shaped the history of our sport.

"It was important that the World Athletics Championships should come to Africa when we had the right host, the right bid and the right circumstances. Nairobi has demonstrated emphatically that this is their moment to supercharge our sport, leaving a compelling legacy that inspires a continent."

Nairobi had submitted a bid for the 2025 edition but lost out to Tokyo, where it finished second in the medal table.

Munich was awarded host status for the 2031 edition of the biennial championships, which takes place in September at the end of the athletics season. It will be the third time Germany has hosted the event but first in the Bavarian capital.

Coe said: "Germany has proved time and again that it is an outstanding and dependable host for major athletics events. Berlin 2009 remains one of the memorable editions of the World Championships, and we have since seen tremendous support for the sport at the European Championships in Berlin and Munich."

However, the decision is a major blow to London, which had been seen as a frontrunner in the race. The UK government threw its weight behind the 2029 bid, with London Stadium - the arena purpose-built for the 2012 Olympics - intended to be the host venue.

But there were challenges even getting it off the ground in the form of needing to smooth relations with Championship football club West Ham, which had earlier argued it had priority to the stadium during the football season.

A deal was reached involving the London mayor's office, Athletic Ventures - a joint venture of UK bodies responsible for organising major events including the London Diamond League - and the Department for Culture, Media and Sport, which satisfied West Ham and meant the bid could go ahead. It was finally submitted last month.

But the public back-and-forth with the club was unlikely to inspire confidence in the World Athletics Council, while sparse crowds at the European Championships in Birmingham's Alexander Stadium this summer - despite being in a different city and in different circumstances - may also have damaged its standing.

Asked whether the West Ham saga played a role in London's failure, Coe refused to comment, saying: "I'm not going to maintain a running commentary today on the judgement and the basis of those judgements."

Jack Buckner, chief executive of UK Athletics and co-founder of Athletic Ventures, said: "We are deeply disappointed that the 2029 World Athletics Championships will not be held in London. We believed we had an outstanding bid which would genuinely take the sport to new levels.

"The UK is an incredible host for major sports events and the British public loves athletics. Athletic Ventures has the ambition to bring those events here and, although today's announcement hasn't gone our way, we will review and regroup. We know the world's athletes love competing here and we'll continue to explore further opportunities to make that happen.

"Our congratulations go to Nairobi and we wish the organising committee all the best for a great event in 2029."

London Stadium has not hosted an athletics championships since a highly successful 2017 edition, when Mo Farah won 10,000m gold and 5,000m silver and Britain took a surprise victory in the men's 4x100m relay. That event broke an eight-year record for ticket sales at a world championships, with more than 660,000 sold.

While the stadium has not hosted another major championships since 2017 it has welcomed the annual London Diamond League. A sellout crowd of 60,000 watched Scot Josh Kerr break the mile world record at this July's meet.

However that success was not enough to persuade World Athletics to choose the capital from the four candidates. London had specifically bid for the 2029 edition, while both Nairobi and Munich had indicated their willingness to host either in 2029 and 2031.

Beijing will host the next edition of the world championships, in 2027.

title: London loses bid to host 2029 World Athletics as Nairobi named host

London has missed out to Nairobi in the bid to host the 2029 World Athletics Championships.

"It was important that the World Athletics Championships should come to Africa when we had the right host, the right bid and the right circumstances. Nairobi has demonstrated emphatically that this is their moment."

The London Stadium, home of Championship club West Ham United, was the proposed host venue for the UK bid.

The stadium was also used for the 2012 Olympic Games and the yearly London Diamond League, and also when the city last hosted the Worlds in 2017.

The UK's bid was led by Athletic Ventures, which consisted of UK Athletics, London Marathon Events and the Great Run Company.

Jack Buckner, CEO of UK Athletics and co-founder of Athletic Ventures, said: "We are deeply disappointed that the 2029 World Athletics Championships will not be held in London. We believed we had an outstanding bid which would genuinely take the sport to new levels.

title: Trump facing AI backlash in Congress as push for guardrails intensifies
description:
President has dismissed anxieties over AI’s dangerous potential even as Democrats and some Republicans acknowledge risks
Donald Trump is facing a rare backlash from the US Congress as Democrats and some Republicans push for guardrails on the world’s most powerful AI companies.
Concerns over the dangerous potential of AI reached fever pitch this week after tech leaders sounded the alarm over the rapid advancement of the technology and its potential threat to humanity.

fullText:
President has dismissed anxieties over AI’s dangerous potential even as Democrats and some Republicans acknowledge risks

Donald Trump is facing a rare backlash from the US Congress as Democrats and some Republicans push for guardrails on the world’s most powerful AI companies.

Concerns over the dangerous potential of AI reached fever pitch this week after tech leaders sounded the alarm over the rapid advancement of the technology and its potential threat to humanity.

Trump dismissed the anxieties on Monday, describing them as a “HOAX” and “conspiracy” and insisting on social media: “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!”

But the 80-year-old president, who has sidelined Congress on numerous issues during his second term, looks increasingly isolated as members of both major parties acknowledged the risks and expressed a desire to act before it was too late.

Don Beyer, a Democratic congressman from Virginia, said: “History will look very poorly on that tweet. He’s not paying attention – or he’s paying attention to the wrong people. He’s being really foolish: not the first time he’s been really foolish but perhaps catastrophically foolish in this case.”

Recent surveys by the University of Maryland’s Program for Public Consultation found 85% of Democrats and 79% of Republicans want a new federal agency to monitor and regulate AI; and 82% of Democrats and 78% of Republicans favour government safety tests for AI making critical decisions.

While many politicians agree on the need to act, they are divided on what government intervention should look like and how far it should go. Some fear a pause on AI development could allow China to take the lead in the AI race and undermine national security.

Beyer called for Congress to stay in session instead of breaking for the midterm elections to work on AI legislation that has already been introduced. “The first thing that I’m very certain of is that the industry shouldn’t be allowed to regulate themselves; history doesn’t support that at all,” he said.

“Especially when they’re making so much money, there will be absolutely no incentive to regulate themselves at a less profit. If we look at medicines or childcare workers or automobile emissions and safety, all throughout our economy, we have regulatory bodies that keep us safe and promote the common good and allow businesses to be profitable. We need something like that.”

The flurry of debate follows warnings last week from three Anthropic researchers that AI could destroy humanity within the next decade. Recent disclosures from several AI companies that their models hacked into outside organizations during botched safety tests have also raised alarm about potential cybersecurity risks, with Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, claiming in an essay that in six to 12 months a “swarm” of AI agents could attack the entire internet and cause hundreds of billions of dollars in damage.

While AI executives have issued their own warnings about the risks from their products, public backlash against the industry and pressure on lawmakers to rein in AI firms have also been mounting throughout the year. The rapid build out of data centers has generated nationwide protests and become a prominent midterm elections issue, while the tech lobby has spent millions in an attempt to influence political campaigns and shape proposed legislation.

The viral panic over AI’s potential existential threat this past week has intensified the longstanding debate over the technology, which so far has resulted in much political handwringing but only a patchwork of attempts at regulation. Many AI experts, regardless of whether they agree on the merits of the Anthropic researchers’ warnings, see this moment as a unique opportunity.

Amba Kak, co-executive director of the AI Now Institute and a former senior adviser on AI for the Federal Trade Commission, said: “You never waste a crisis is an old and well-worn adage in policy land. We’re looking at a really important policy opportunity and a policy window.”

AI industry leaders have also suggested that they are open to increased oversight and the formation of some kind of standards body, while Amodei’s letter advocated for international cooperation with states like China akin to cold war-era arms limitation treaties. Many AI regulation advocates are skeptical of industry proposals, however, arguing that AI companies are attempting to undercut strict government oversight and set their own terms.

In a rare intervention on Monday night, former president Barack Obama welcomed the current debate but warned that “at the end of the day, voluntary standards made by a handful of tech companies won’t be enough”.

Writing on X, Obama added: “We need government – and specifically our leaders in Washington – to get proactive in coming up with concrete proposals, laws and regulations that deal with serious safety concerns, anticipate AI’s impact on jobs and our kids, and make sure that AI’s benefits are widely spread.”

Members of Congress are holding a series of meetings this week with AI researchers and safety advocates as Congress tries to address the growing alarm. The Senate Democratic leader, Chuck Schumer, urged the Trump administration to provide a classified briefing to senators on AI and work with members of Congress and industry leaders to implement guardrails and block China from accessing the US’s advanced AI chips.

Bernie Sanders, who announced a bill last week aimed at banning “artificial superintelligence,” is holding a private briefing this week for other senators. The briefing will include co-founder of the Future of Life Institute co-founder Max Tegmark, whose organization has become one of the most well-funded and politically connected voices in warning about AI’s alleged existential risks.

Tegmark said: “Every other industry in the US used to be unregulated. There used to be soothing syrup fed to infants with opioids in it. Then the FDA was created, now stuff like that doesn’t reach the market. Eventually safety standards came in. That hasn’t happened with AI companies.”

Congressman Greg Casar, a Democrat who will speak with Sanders at the Future of Life Institute’s “Pro-Human Assembly” on Tuesday, dismissed the notion that big tech companies should be responsible for AI safety. “That’s like saying it should be bank robbers that are responsible for bank safety,” he said. “The American people are waking up to the dangers of unregulated artificial intelligence.

“You have these AI CEOs coming to take away people’s jobs, to surveil people and attack our freedoms, and now you have all of these whistleblowers talking about potential mass casualty events. So Congress should be cracking down on these big tech companies and on these AI CEOs, not like what Republican Speaker Mike Johnson and Donald Trump go and do. They go to these AI CEOs and ask for Super Pac checks for their candidates.”

Republicans broke from Trump in acknowledging the potential perils of AI but came up with a variety of different fixes for the problem. Congressman Jay Obernolte of California, the lead Republican negotiating a bipartisan bill to govern AI, said: “We need to avoid overregulation, so we need to achieve these two conflicting goals … of protecting Americans against very real risks of AI in the hands of malicious human actors, while at the same time balancing the need to have a light-touch regulatory environment that allows the positive benefits of AI to improve our economy and our society. So that’s that’s the difficult part is getting that balance right.”

John Kennedy, a Republican senator for Louisiana, said he would propose a bill on Wednesday to require all AI companies build a kill switch into their models. “It’s not going to put the federal government in charge of the kill switch. They would be in charge of their own kill switch, but they all have to have a kill switch, and I’m going to put that on the floor.”

But despite the growing urgency and public pressure, some members suspect that the bitterly polarised Congress will not be able to meet the moment.

Congressman Jared Moskowitz, a Democrat from Florida, was sceptical about the possibility of passing an AI regulation bill. “I think Congress has already shown they don’t have the capacity,” he said. “The speaker has said, ‘we’re not going to do anything’. In fact, he has said ‘we don’t know enough to do it’. I think that’s not what the American people are looking for. The American people are looking for leadership.”

Rick Scott, a Republican senator for Florida, added: “Did we balance the budget? Oh, did we pass a budget? See, what have we gotten done? So you think we’re going to get AI done?

“By the way, these companies that create a product that they think can destroy mankind – they have a responsibility to do it themselves. They shouldn’t be relying on us. I mean, it’s disgusting. I saw this as governor. People come, ‘go regulate me’. Yeah, we know what they want is they don’t want to be responsible for their actions.”

fullText:
Beijing hits back after Anthropic CEO calls for US to impede China’s progress in AI

China has dismissed what it said were “fearmongering” calls for the US to block Beijing’s AI industry, even as the top Chinese spy chief warned the evolving technology could threaten Communist party rule.

The US tech entrepreneur and Anthropic chief executive, Dario Amodei, wrote an essay published over the weekend that called for a global slowdown in AI capabilities, but also said Washington should actively impede Beijing’s advancement in order to keep a technological edge.

Warning that AI could give the Chinese Communist party a chance “to militarily dominate democracies”, Amodei said he believed “a Chinese lead in AI would pose grave danger for the US and the world”.

China’s ministry of foreign affairs responded to a question about Amodei’s essay by saying all parties should work together on AI.

“Fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance, which serves no one’s interest,” spokesperson Guo Jiakun said at a press conference on Monday.

In his essay, Amodei predicted that a swarm of AI “agents” could take over the internet in six to 12 months unless researchers agree to slow down. He said that while “global pacing will require cooperation with China”, steps were needed to “keep democracies’ AI lead over autocracies as large as possible”.

Other tech bosses, including the OpenAI CEO, Sam Altman, the Google DeepMind chair, Demis Hassabis, and the SpaceX chief, Elon Musk, have posted general support for Amodei’s lengthy essay, although not specifically on China.

While Beijing rejects its dominance in AI would be dangerous, it does share fears over the pace of development. The president of China, Xi Jinping, warned at a conference in July that AI should “always remain under human control”.

But the extent of the Chinese government’s concerns was shown in an article published on Sunday in the state-run magazine China Cyberspace, in which the country’s top intelligence official wrote that the technology could threaten the government’s hold on power.

The head of China’s ministry of state security, Chen Yixin, wrote that “hostile forces and individuals with ulterior motives” were abusing AI to wage a “propaganda war and a cognitive war against us, directly threatening our political security, institutional security, and ideological security”.

Chen referred specifically to US models such as Anthropic’s Claude and OpenAI’s GPT-5.5-Cyber models, which he said have been weaponised and were examples of new threats to cybersecurity.

While the public, governments and tech bosses are now warning of the dangers of AI, Donald Trump has dismissed such concerns outright. On Monday, the US president said the only “guardrails” that AI needed were a “STRONG AND SMART” president.

Trump has been particularly sensitive to stock market changes, and AI stocks have slipped after concerns over the pace of AI growth were raised.

The US and Chinese leaders are expected to discuss AI governance, among other topics, at a meeting planned on 24 September.

In an editorial published Sunday, China’s state-run Global Times newspaper dismissed Amodei’s essay as a veiled call to “contain” China.

“The article is packed with containment provisions targeting China and is, in essence, a ‘cold war playbook’ for the AI sector,” it said.

The Associated Press contributed to this report

title: If You Love 'The Paper,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next
description: Another hilarious comedy set in the world of journalism.
fullText:
The Paper isn’t exactly a sequel to The Office—despite existing in the same universe and sharing the character Oscar Nuñez (played by Office alum Oscar Martinez), the show is its own animal. Unlike Michael Scott, Ned Sampson (Domhnall Gleeson) has a noble quest in saving the Toledo Truth Teller from the sad fate facing most local newspapers, and that shift in focus gives The Paper its own identity. And yet it’s as hilarious as The Office ever was, filled with the same mockumentary-inspired spit-takes and ridiculous capers (largely thanks to Esmeralda, played by Sabrina Impacciatore, who is kind of like Michael and Dwight rolled into one spectacular character).

If you’ve already torn through the show’s first two seasons and you’ve watched all the streamalike shows out there, then the next move is obvious: Watch the 1994 film The Paper.

Although they share a title, there’s no direct connection between the show and the movie—but they’re more similar than you might think. Both are focused on the slow, grinding decline of journalism in America; Ned wants to return the Truth Teller to something resembling a real newspaper, and metro editor Henry Hackett (Michael Keaton) wants to save The New York Sun from (you guessed it) steep budget cuts and an ownership more interested in monetizing its assets than great journalism.

1994’s The Paper, directed by Ron Howard and co-written by David Koepp and his brother Stephen (then an editor at Time Magazine), has a very different style of comedy from The Paper’s mockumentary approach—it’s rougher, edgier, and comes from the fast-paced, motor-mouthed screwball comedy tradition. But it’s just as funny, from the swirl of overheard conversations in the busy newsroom (this is a film that rewards multiple viewings to catch all the little jokes) to the way Keaton’s performance edges closer and closer to Beetlejuice territory as the pressure on Henry mounts (seriously, by the end of the infamous phone-call scene, he’s basically channeling the undead bio-exorcist).

If you’re looking for a comedy like the Peacock show, one that celebrates both journalism and the human beings who think it matters, you’ll definitely love this movie. Plus, it’s got a stacked cast: Aside from Keaton operating at his absolute peak, you’ve got Glenn Close, Robert Duvall, and Marisa Tomei, and Jason Alexander and Catherine O’Hara in small but memorable roles. And if the sort of big tabloid newspaper like The New York Sun is almost extinct these days, that’s part of what makes the movie so effective—just like the series, it starts with the assumption that these papers and the people who work at them matter, and are worth celebrating. Rent The Paper on Prime Video.

Need more journalistic levity than The Paper (and The Paper) can provide? Read on for more movie suggestions that fans of the show will love.

A massive critical and box-office hit in 1987, James L. Brooks' Broadcast News is more of a dramedy than a straightforward comedy—though it has many hilarious moments, including the scene where aspiring news anchor Aaron (Albert Brooks) can’t stop sweating during his big chance on camera. Holly Hunter plays a sharp producer torn between her journalistic ethics and her attraction to a slick but not particularly bright (or ethical) new anchor, played by a hilariously befuddled William Hurt. Its journalistic setting and its concerns over an institution being destroyed by corporate interests and abandoned principles will resonate with fans of The Paper—and it’s a terrific movie in general. Rent Broadcast News on Prime Video.

Want another comedy set in the offices of a struggling newspaper? Check out this forgotten classic from director Joan Micklin Silver (Crossing Delancey). In the mid-1970s, The Back Bay Mainline is a local alternative newspaper struggling to transition from its activist origins to a more mature business. The offices are shabby, the staff underpaid (a truly funny Jeff Goldblum plays music critic Max Arloft, who notes at one point that he takes home $75 a week, which would be about $11k per year in 2026 money), and the question of whether their revolutionary days actually achieved anything hangs in the air as a corporate takeover looms on the horizon. The humor is more subtle and the gender politics are, well, what you might expect from 1976—but there’s charm to spare. Stream Between the Lines on Kanopy or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you want fast-paced, crackling humor with a newspaper backdrop, this all-timer is a must-watch. When newspaper editor Walter Burns (Cary Grant in Ultra Cary Grant Mode) discovers his best reporter (and ex-wife), Hildy (Rosalind Russell), is not only getting married but also leaving her career, he decides to win her back and keep her at the paper. He asks her to cover one last story while doing everything he can to ruin her new relationship and convince her that she’s meant to be a reporter—and with him. The dialogue is incredibly fast, very funny, and any fan of The Paper will love it. Stream His Gal Friday on The Roku Channel, Kanopy, Hoopla, or Fubo, or rent it on Prime Video.

This sweet, funny romantic comedy follows Becky Fuller (Rachel McAdams), who accepts a job as producer at struggling morning show DayBreak. Finding the production in chaos, she uses contractual magic to force veteran newscaster Mike Pomeroy (a crusty Harrison Ford) to become the show’s co-host alongside Colleen Peck (Diane Keaton), to his horror. The battle of wills between Becky and Mike, the battle to save the show, and Becky’s struggle to be taken seriously by the men around her (including her love interest, fellow producer Adam (Patrick Wilson), are packed with sharp jokes and observations about the modern age of news and media—perfect for fans of The Paper. Stream Morning Glory on Kanopy or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

Any time fans of a mockumentary-style comedy go looking for a movie, they will eventually find their way to one of Christopher Guest’s classic entries. For fans of The Paper, the best choice from that list is Best in Show. Co-written with Schitt’s Creek’s Eugene Levy, the setting (a national dog show) couldn’t be further from a tiny Midwest newspaper, but the vibe and joke structures are the same, with “talking head” interviews delivering plenty of belly laughs from folks who are so deep in the sauce of their subculture they don’t see how bizarre it looks to outsiders—but, just like Ned’s belief in the power of journalism, underneath all the jokes is a sweet sincerity. If your favorite part about The Paper is the documentary conceit, check this one out. Stream Best in Show on The Roku Channel, Plex, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

title: Why Team India player was penalised after Women's Asia Cup final
description: India pacer Kranti Gaud admitted the offence and accepted the sanction proposed by Supriya Rani Das of the Emirates ICC International Panel of Match Referees. As a result, there was no need for a formal hearing.
fullText:
NEW DELHI: India pacer Kranti Gaud has been fined 10 per cent of her match fee for breaching the ICC Code of Conduct during the Women's Asia Cup final against Sri Lanka in Dubai on Sunday.

Gaud was found guilty of a Level 1 breach of the ICC Code of Conduct for Players and Player Support Personnel.

Gaud breached Article 2.5 of the ICC Code of Conduct, which relates to "using language, actions or gestures which disparage, or which could provoke an aggressive reaction from a batter upon his/her dismissal during an International Match."

The incident took place in the first over of Sri Lanka's innings. After dismissing opener Imesha Dulani, Gaud gestured in the direction of the pavilion.

Gaud admitted the offence and accepted the sanction proposed by Supriya Rani Das of the Emirates ICC International Panel of Match Referees. As a result, there was no need for a formal hearing.

On-field umpires Saleema Imtiaz and Shathira Jakir Jesy, third umpire Rokeya Sultana and fourth umpire Humaira Farah levelled the charge.

Along with the 10 per cent fine, one demerit point has been added to Gaud's disciplinary record.

It was her first offence in a 24-month period.

Level 1 breaches carry a minimum penalty of an official reprimand and a maximum penalty of 50 per cent of a player's match fee. They can also result in one or two demerit points.

Pakistan have been fined five per cent of their match fee for maintaining a slow over-rate during their Women's Asia Cup semifinal against Sri Lanka on Friday.

G.S. Lakshmi of the Emirates ICC International Panel of Match Referees imposed the sanction after Pakistan were found to be one over short of the target after time allowances were taken into consideration.

Under Article 2.22 of the ICC Code of Conduct for Players and Player Support Personnel, which deals with minimum over-rate offences, players are fined five per cent of their match fee for every over their team fails to bowl in the allotted time.

Pakistan captain Fatima Sana pleaded guilty to the offence and accepted the proposed sanction. Therefore, there was no need for a formal hearing.

On-field umpires Vrinda Rathi and Shathira Jakir Jesy, third umpire Rokeya Sultana and fourth umpire Rabab Ahsan levelled the charge.

title: Maldini driving licence suspended after car crash
description: Italy international Daniel Maldini has his driving licence suspended following a car crash in Milan.
fullText:
Italy international Daniel Maldini has had his driving licence suspended after he was found to be over the legal alcohol limit following a car crash in Milan.

Maldini, son of Italy and AC Milan legend Paolo and grandson of the similarly feted Cesare, was one among six people to suffer minor injuries after his Porsche Carrera 4 collided with another vehicle in the early hours of Sunday.

The attacking midfielder had scored the winning goal for Cagliari in a 2-1 win against his parent club Atalanta in Serie A just hours before the accident.

Milan city police confirmed to BBC Sport that there had been a road traffic accident involving the 24-year-old footballer.

It said: "Mr Maldini was administered a breathalyser test at the scene" and his "driving license was confiscated following a positive result".

He was taken to hospital for precautionary checks before being released.

According to reports, an initial breath test carried out by the police at the scene of the accident recorded a blood alcohol level of 0.91 grams per litre, while a second reading registered 0.89 g/l - both higher than Italy's legal limit of 0.5 g/l.

In a statement, Cagliari said Maldini had "undergone toxicological screening following recent media reports" and that "all tests returned negative results".

The club added Maldini will join the squad for training on Monday to prepare for the team's forthcoming fixtures.

Maldini became became the third generation of his family to play for Italy when he made his debut against Israel in a Nations League fixture in 2024.

He has made six appearances for his country, with the latest coming in September 2025.

title: Davey reignites international ambitions with Wales
description: Uncapped Wales scrum-half Megan Davey's admits she almost called it quits before her recent call-up at the age of 26.
fullText:
Megan Davey's international ambitions have been reignited at her self-proclaimed 'old' age of 26.

Loughborough Lightning's record appearance holder considered going into full-time teaching when she did not make Wales' 2026 Six Nations squad.

Her hopes were dashed again when omitted from Sean Lynn's extended training squad for the WXV Global Series.

"There was a little bit of a wobble," admitted uncapped Davey.

"It's hard to keep going when you're at my age, you feel old in the game."

But the half-back received a call-up last month and is now part of the 39-strong squad which will take on South Africa, USA and Japan.

"There's always been something inside me, I know I can do it, it's the voice inside my head that's kept me going," she said.

"I was really happy that I got an opportunity."

Rose out of Wales WXV squad with injury

Davey qualifies for Wales through her grandfather from Llanelli but went through the English pathway system as a youngster.

"The avenue for under-20s was always really with England because it wasn't as set up with Wales, but now it's really good," she said.

"I'm a little bit older... now I feel like I can really do people proud."

And despite being a latecomer in camp, Davey says everyone has been welcoming.

"There's always that thing when you walk into an environment that's already established, you're like 'how am I going to do?' but I was really raring to go," she added.

"Obviously a bit sad that I wasn't in the squad to begin with, but you just crack on with what you're doing."

Live on BBC One, iPlayer and the BBC Sport website and app, with live text coverage

Davey has primarily trained at scrum-half with Wales and faces competition from Keira Bevan and Seren Lockwood.

And contrary to the stereotype of the position, the nines get along with no animosity.

"We all really enjoy each other's company. We want each other to do well, so there's never that hatred towards each other," said Davey, who has previously started at fly-half for Loughborough.

"Whoever goes out there and does the job first is the best pick for the team and you just need to back that completely."

Wales open their WXV campaign against South Africa at Cardiff Arms Park on Friday, 18 September (19:15 BST), and any potential involvement would mean the world to Davey.

"Playing international rugby is such a privilege and I want to make everyone proud - my family, but also the coaches that have been behind me for the last 15 years of my journey," she said.

"It's just that final step, like 'I made it'. I'm really excited and hopefully it comes at some point."
